cap.convergent: Oceanic plate sinks beneath a continent. Coral flashes are earthquakes tracing the slab down to ~700 km.
cap.divergent: Plates pull apart; rising magma freezes into new crust and records alternating magnetic stripes.
cap.transform: Plates slide horizontally. Stress builds where the boundary locks, then releases in earthquakes.
cap.normal: Stretching: the hanging wall slides down the fault.
cap.reverse: Compression: the hanging wall is pushed up and over.
cap.strike: Shear: the blocks slide sideways and the road is offset.
cap.P: P wave · ≈ 6 km/s · rock compresses along the direction of travel. Follow the coral particle.
cap.S: S wave · ≈ 3.5 km/s · rock shears at right angles to travel. Follow the coral particle.
cap.R: Rayleigh surface wave · ≈ 3 km/s · the ground rolls in ellipses that fade with depth.
cap.tsunami: Speed = √(g × depth). Watch the wave slow down and grow taller as the sea shallows.

mag.area_note: Circle area = energy released. Each step ≈ 32× more.

depth.omori: Aftershocks per day after a mainshock (Omori’s law)

feltmap.title: How felt maps work
feltmap.how_1: Felt maps are made automatically from how people use sisma in the 3 minutes after an earthquake. When a quake is felt, people nearby open the app at the same moment, and that rush of activity shows where it was probably felt.
feltmap.how_2: While sisma is open and you have allowed location, it can send an approximate position to our servers about once a minute. Before it leaves your device it is moved randomly by up to 500 m, and it carries no account, device or IP identifier.
feltmap.how_3: We only show areas of about 10 km where at least 3 people opened the app more than usual, so nothing on the map can be tied to a person. Positions are deleted after 7 days, never shared, and never used for anything else.
feltmap.how_4: You can turn this off at any time in Me. Felt maps are an estimate, not an official intensity map.

data.title: Data
data.card_sub: Live charts of worldwide earthquake activity from the USGS catalog.
data.lead: Live charts of worldwide earthquakes from the USGS catalog: how many, how strong, how deep, where, and how this compares with the long-term record.
data.locked_p: The charts on this page are part of sisma+. The explanations are free to read.
data.signin_p: Sign in and start sisma+ to see the live charts.
data.error: The data couldn’t be loaded. Please try again later.
data.activity_p: How many M4.5+ earthquakes were recorded worldwide, per hour or per day. M4.5 is the size the USGS aims to record everywhere in the world, so these counts are comparable across regions.
data.mag_p: The last 30 days in half-magnitude steps. Smaller earthquakes are far more common than large ones; seismologists describe this with the Gutenberg–Richter relationship.
data.depth_p: Where the earthquakes started, in the USGS depth classes. Most are shallow; intermediate and deep earthquakes happen where one plate sinks beneath another.
data.region_p: Earthquakes in the last 30 days by world region (the same regions as the region filter). Regions are geographic, not tectonic.
data.energy_p: The estimated energy released, added up day by day over 30 days. Each step of one magnitude means about 32 times more energy, so a few large earthquakes release most of it.
data.energy_top: The largest earthquake (M{mag}) released about {pct}% of this energy.
data.history_p: Large earthquakes are recorded reliably over the whole period, so this count can be compared year by year. The dashed line is the average of the complete years; this year is still in progress.
data.ring_on: Mostly on the Ring of Fire
data.note_1: More earthquakes on record does not mean more earthquakes: there are many more seismometers than in the past, so more small earthquakes are detected. The number of M7+ earthquakes has stayed fairly constant.
data.note_2: Recent earthquakes are preliminary. Agencies revise locations and magnitudes as more data arrive, so recent counts can change.
data.note_3: Even at M4.5, the USGS list is not a complete record of every earthquake worldwide, especially where there are few stations.
data.note_4: Energy is estimated from magnitude with a standard formula (log₁₀ E = 1.5 M + 4.8, in joules). It is an approximation, not a measurement.
data.note_5: A busy day or week does not, by itself, mean a large earthquake is coming.
